title: Study Abroad Experience at Duke University and Lund University
paragraphs: In April 2017 I was given the opportunity to do clerkships for four weeks each at Duke University in the United States, and in May at Lund University in Sweden. Below I report what I experienced and felt.

[Life in Durham] As described above, on weekdays I did my clerkship at the hospital with a sense of tension, but after returning home and on weekends I devoted myself to refreshing. My host family, Fred and Jenny, were kind and gentle people, and they took me by car to a barbecue restaurant, a North Carolina specialty, and to the woods while walking their two dogs. Durham was a green countryside town ideal for strolling, but the drawbacks were that it was unexpectedly hot and humid and inconvenient without a car. However, because the airport is nearby it was easy to travel, and I may have been busier than on weekdays, flying to Boston with a classmate who was staying with me for research study abroad, joining two students from Johns Hopkins to sightsee in New York, being treated to Japanese food after a long time at the home of a Japanese doctor who used to be in a Nagoya University laboratory, and watching a minor league baseball game.

[People I Met] In the hospital I met many students and residents from other countries, and I was overwhelmed by their ambition and drive to improve. The Lebanese student who did the clerkship with me had come in order to obtain letters of recommendation for applying to US residencies in the future, and was excellent in everything: English proficiency, knowledge, presentation ability and how to appeal to others. I just wanted to crawl into a hole, but I decided to make efforts to grow in my own way, and in my free time I searched for papers and went early in the morning to read through the charts. What I keenly felt during the clerkship was that, even though I knew I could ask about anything I did not understand, I could not even do that unless I could hear the English and had a certain amount of knowledge as a premise. Conversely, if one has knowledge one can learn more deeply, and that has led to higher motivation for study after returning to Japan. In addition, the patients and their families treated even students without showing displeasure. To me, whose expression was stiff with tension during examinations, they spoke with jokes or said "You look better when you smile!", and I feel that far from being unable to do anything, I was in fact encouraged by the patients. And in the last week of the clerkship I visited to observe an operation by the neurosurgeon Dr. 福島孝則. I heard many surprising things, such as that anesthesia management during surgery is done by nurses and that there are endoscopy nurses who harvest the great saphenous vein for bypass endoscopically. What was most impressive was Dr. 福島's personality: his attitude of speaking up to and asserting himself to others in any language, his knowledge of medical education and healthcare systems in various countries, his approachability in holding meals to which he invites patients' families and students, and his humility in always carrying mini-size origami and not neglecting to train his fingers. I felt that all of these must be the factors that have made Dr. 福島 a world-top-level surgeon. I too felt I want to become able to see the world with a broad perspective.

[Clerkship in Radiology at Lund University] I left the United States at the end of April and moved in May to Lund University in southern Sweden to do the clerkship. Lund University is a relatively new partner university, and I was anxious because it is in a non-English-speaking country, but it turned out to be a very enjoyable and fulfilling stay. The radiology department is a large unit to which 50 doctors alone belong, and it was subdivided into sections. From among them I rotated through chest, abdomen, pediatric/musculoskeletal and neuro for one week each. The mornings began with joint conferences with other departments, and after they ended I followed senior doctors to be taught the key points of image reading and to observe interesting tests and treatments. In the abdominal and neuro divisions many IVR procedures such as TACE and cerebral thrombectomy were also performed, so I was often in the angiography room for hours. The charts and conferences were in Swedish, and it was quite difficult to follow the conferences, but I somehow got through by guessing the meaning relying on medical terms similar to English and by asking for explanations of the cases before and after the conferences. Above all, the staff were kind and explained and conversed in English, so I think I hardly had any trouble from not knowing Swedish. What I felt was typically Swedish was, first, that they always take a coffee break (fika in Swedish). In the large lounge dedicated to radiology, I could talk with various doctors over sweets and coffee. And that after 4 p.m. the day-shift doctors go home promptly. Some doctors take Friday afternoons off, or take a block of leave by the week and go on vacation, and I felt it was quite different from Japan. What surprised me was the story that women make up more than half of the doctors in Sweden. With childcare services well developed, many stay-at-home fathers, and parental leave that both spouses must take, I felt a fundamental difference in the system, as well as in awareness. Conversely, a resident there (raising two children) asked me, puzzled, why are there so few women doctors in Japan? How do they manage both?

[Life in Lund] From the time I arrived in early May, the hours of daylight grew longer day by day, and in June it was so bright that one lost the sense of time, with sunrise at 4:30 and sunset at 22:00. In addition to the green and beautiful townscape, there was no trouble with meals or shopping, and it was a convenient place where one could go by train to play in other cities right away; prices were a little high, but it was a very comfortable environment. However, although there were many international students, compared with the United States they were mostly Westerners, and Asians seem rare. During the clerkship I stayed in a dormitory for international students, where we exchanged information while preparing dinner in the shared kitchen and held parties bringing food. Most people had come to take a master's in their respective majors, and some planned to look for jobs in Sweden. I also met again a student who had come from Lund to Nagoya University while I was still in Japan, and I was looked after by being shown around the hospital and told about delicious restaurants. I resolved to treat foreigners and international students in Japan kindly.

[People I Met] There were several doctors who had entered Swedish medical schools from other European countries or who had graduated from medical school in their own countries and then worked in Sweden. They said that, while troubled by the language barrier, they had moved because they were attracted by Sweden's well-developed welfare and good working environment. Many people were also interested in Japan, and I could enjoy conversations on various topics, such as Japanese food like sushi and ramen, an amusing Japanese runner in the marathon at the Stockholm Olympics (I did not know at all, but when I looked it up he was on Wikipedia too), and where I would recommend going when they go to Japan on their next vacation.

[Summary] Although the periods were short, one month each, it was a very good experience to be able to do clinical clerkships in two countries. The differences in culture, ways of thinking and ways of working that I glimpsed while staying in each country were very interesting. One of my motives for applying to study abroad was that I wanted to challenge myself to see how much I could do in an environment with many barriers, a clerkship at a prestigious overseas university. As a result, these two months made me understand well the shortcomings and lacks in myself that I had not seen before. Preparing as much as possible, interacting actively with people, and casting off shame to ask and absorb everything: I think these are necessary also after I start working. Saying it like this may make it sound like a hard experience, but of course there were also many fun and happy experiences that I could not have had without studying abroad. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the professors of the International Collaboration Office, everyone in the Academic Affairs Division, the seniors who gave me advice, my classmates who encouraged each other, and my friends and family who supported me. Thank you very much. With the resident and the Lebanese exchange student at Duke University. Thai food party at the dormitory
